title: Taking a Simple Order
subtitle: How to ask for quantity, confirm details, and process an order in clear English
description: Taking an order is one of the most common moments in sales. This lesson teaches you the simple, direct language you need: how to ask how many a customer wants, how to check availability, confirm the total, and close the order professionally.
dialogueSubtitle: Marcus is ready to buy — Riley takes his order step by step

vocabulary.definition: A request to buy a specific product or service. When a customer places an order, they confirm they want to buy.
vocabulary.example: Marcus called Riley and said: I want to place an order for fifteen units of the Standard Plan. Riley said: Perfect — I will process your order now.

vocabulary.definition: The number or amount of something. In sales, quantity means how many units or items the customer wants to buy.
vocabulary.example: Riley asked Marcus: What quantity do you need? Marcus said: We need fifteen — one for each person on the team.

vocabulary.definition: To say yes and make something certain. When you confirm an order, both sides agree on the details.
vocabulary.example: Riley checked all the details and said: Shall I confirm your order? Marcus said: Yes — fifteen units, delivery on Friday.

vocabulary.definition: One single item in an order. When companies buy software or products, they often count in units.
vocabulary.example: Marcus said: We have fifteen people on our team, so we need fifteen units. Riley said: Fifteen units — I will check if they are all available.

vocabulary.definition: Ready to buy or use right now. If a product is available, the customer can order it today.
vocabulary.example: Marcus asked if the plan was ready. Riley said: Let me check — yes, fifteen units are available. We can deliver them by Friday.

vocabulary.definition: The process of sending products to the customer after they order. In B2B sales, delivery can also mean when software access is set up.
vocabulary.example: Marcus asked: When can you deliver? Riley said: When would you like delivery? We can have everything ready by the end of the week.

vocabulary.definition: The final amount — the full price after counting all units. We say 'your total comes to' when we give the final price.
vocabulary.example: Riley confirmed the price clearly: Your total comes to $750 for fifteen units. That is $50 per unit per month.

vocabulary.definition: To handle or complete something officially. When you process an order, you start preparing it and send a confirmation.
vocabulary.example: Marcus said he was ready. Riley said: I will process that for you now — you will receive a confirmation email in a few minutes.

phrasalVerbs.definition: The key question for taking an order. Use 'many' — not 'much' — because you are counting individual units. Always ask this before confirming any details.
phrasalVerbs.example: Marcus said he wanted to buy the Standard Plan. Riley responded: Great — how many would you like? We need to know the quantity before we can process anything.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: Let me check if that is available
phrasalVerbs.definition: A professional way to verify that you have the product in stock before confirming. It shows you are careful and organised — never promise what you have not checked.
phrasalVerbs.example: Marcus asked for twenty units. Riley said: Let me check if that is available. She looked at the system and said: Yes — twenty units are ready for you.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Use this when all the details are agreed. It is a polite, professional way to close the conversation and move to the next step.
phrasalVerbs.example: Riley had the quantity, the price, and the delivery date. She said: Shall I confirm your order? Marcus said: Yes, go ahead.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Ask this after you confirm the quantity and availability. It shows you are organised and ready to complete the order.
phrasalVerbs.example: Marcus confirmed fifteen units. Riley then asked: When would you like delivery? Marcus said: We need it by the end of next week.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Use this to state the final price. Always say 'your total comes to' — not 'the price is' or 'it costs'. It sounds professional and clear.
phrasalVerbs.example: Riley confirmed the order details and said: Your total comes to $750 for fifteen units. That is the final price, including everything.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: I will process that for you now
phrasalVerbs.definition: Say this to close the order professionally. It tells the customer that the work is starting and they will hear back soon.
phrasalVerbs.example: Marcus confirmed everything. Riley said: Perfect — I will process that for you now. You will receive a confirmation email within a few minutes.

completeSentenceExercise.instructions: Choose the correct word to complete each sentence. Only one answer is correct.

items.explanation: Use 'many' for things you can count, like units, people, or items. 'Much' is for things you cannot count, like time or water.

items.sentence: Let me check if that is _____.
items.explanation: 'Available' means ready to buy or use. 'Free' means it costs nothing — a very different meaning. 'Open' does not work for products.

items.sentence: Your total _____ to $750 for fifteen units.
items.explanation: 'Your total comes to' is the fixed phrase we use in sales. 'Adds' and 'goes' are not used this way.
'Delivery' is the standard business word for when and how products arrive. 'Shipping' is also used but 'delivery' is more common in B2B conversations.
'Confirm' means to make something official and certain. 'Check' means to look at something — it does not close the order. 'Make' is too informal.

items.sentence: I will _____ that for you now.
items.explanation: 'Process' is the professional word for completing an order officially. 'Handle' and 'do' are too casual for this context.

chooseResponse.instructions: Read what the customer says. Choose the best response from the three options.

items.customerLine: We need fifty units. Do you have them in stock?
options: Let me check if that is available — I will confirm in a moment.
items.explanation: Option B responds to the question by checking availability — exactly what the customer asked. Option A asks for quantity the customer already gave. Option C jumps to pricing before confirming stock.

items.customerLine: Okay, we are ready to place the order.
options: Let me check if that is available.
items.explanation: Option C is the right next step — the customer is ready, so you confirm the order. Option A checks availability, which should have been done earlier. Option B asks for quantity, which the customer has already given.

items.customerLine: What is the total price for thirty units?
items.explanation: Option A answers the question directly with the final price. Option B moves to confirmation before answering the pricing question. Option C asks about delivery — too early before the customer knows the price.

spotTheMistake.instructions: Read the conversation. Three lines have a mistake. Can you find them?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Hi. We need some units of the Standard Plan.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Twenty units. Are they free right now?

dialogue.speaker: Alex
dialogue.text: Yes, twenty units are available. When would you like delivery?

dialogue.speaker: Alex
dialogue.text: Your price comes to $1,000 for twenty units.

mistakes.explanation: Use 'many' for countable things like units, people, or items. 'Much' is for things you cannot count, like time or money.
'Available' means ready to buy or use. 'Free' means it costs nothing — a very different meaning that would confuse the customer.
The correct phrase is 'your total comes to'. 'Price' is not wrong in general, but 'total' is the professional sales phrase used when giving a final amount.
